WHAT YOU ALREADY KNOW   What you already know
Book 2, Chapter 9 compared absorption and variable costing. Chapter 5 of this book prepared a flexible budget in contribution format; Chapter 7 budgeted the cost of goods manufactured.

WORKED EXAMPLE   Worked example: cost of goods sold for 2028
Beginning stock 42,000 cases × $12.60 = $529,200; plus cost of goods manufactured $11,350,600; minus ending stock 43,000 cases × $12.60 = $541,800. Cost of goods sold is $11,338,000, as Figure F308-03 shows.
Less fixed overhead applied above budget

EXAM TRAP   Manufactured is not sold
Cost of goods manufactured is the cost of cases finished; cost of goods sold is the cost of cases sold. An answer that uses one for the other ignores the change in finished goods.

WORKED EXAMPLE   Worked example: a commission plan
The sales director proposes raising commissions by $0.30 a case and cutting sales salaries by $200,000, expecting 20,000 extra cases. The contribution margin per case falls to $7.90. Figure F308-08 shows that operating income still rises by $88,000.

EXAM TRAP   Which costs go above the line?
Variable selling costs reduce the contribution margin; fixed selling and administrative costs do not. Deducting marketing or salaries before the contribution margin, or leaving out freight and commissions, gives the wrong margin.

WORKED EXAMPLE   Everything ties
Quarters: $702,000 + $795,000 + $888,000 + $795,000 = $3,180,000; + $2,000 at year end = $3,182,000.
$3,182,000 − $3,180,000 = $2,000, the fixed overhead in the rise in stock.
